reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and autoinflammatory disease consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disorder caused by biallelic variants in MVK, reducing mevalonate kinase activity in the cholesterol and isoprenoid pathway
Presents in infancy or early childhood with recurrent febrile episodes lasting several days, often triggered by vaccination, infection or stress
Attacks feature high fever with cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea, arthralgia and a polymorphous rash
Aphthous oral ulceration and painful hepatosplenomegaly are common during flares
Serum IgD is often elevated, giving the historical name hyper-IgD syndrome, though a normal IgD does not exclude the diagnosis
The severe end of the spectrum, mevalonic aciduria, adds developmental delay, dysmorphism, ataxia, cataract and failure to thrive
Urinary mevalonic acid is markedly raised during attacks, especially in the severe form
IL-1 inhibition is the mainstay of treatment for frequent or severe flares, with enzyme activity and genetic testing confirming the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Mevalonate kinase deficiency results from biallelic variants in MVK that reduce the activity of mevalonate kinase, an enzyme of the isoprenoid biosynthetic pathway downstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Impaired production of non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, disrupts prenylation of small GTPases and activates the inflammasome, driving excess interleukin-1 beta release. The degree of residual enzyme activity determines whether the phenotype is the milder periodic fever (hyper-IgD) syndrome or severe mevalonic aciduria.
additionalDifferentials: PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Urinary organic acids for mevalonic acid, ideally during an attack
Serum immunoglobulins including IgD and IgA
Acute-phase reactants and full blood count during and between flares
Ophthalmological and developmental assessment in suspected severe disease
redFlags: Features of secondary amyloidosis such as proteinuria in long-standing uncontrolled disease
Severe neurological impairment, ataxia or visual loss suggesting mevalonic aciduria
Failure to thrive with recurrent crises in infancy
Signs of macrophage activation syndrome during a severe flare
reference.prognosis: The milder periodic fever form tends to improve with age but can be complicated by secondary amyloidosis if inflammation is poorly controlled. Mevalonic aciduria carries a poor prognosis with significant neurodevelopmental disability and early mortality; IL-1 blockade can substantially reduce flare frequency.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgD is normal
Missing the raised urinary mevalonic acid by sampling only between attacks
Overlooking the risk of secondary amyloidosis with chronic inflammation
Failing to distinguish the severe (mevalonic aciduria) form, which needs broader multisystem care
references: OMIM: Hyper-IgD syndrome and mevalonic aciduria
management: Control the autoinflammatory febrile attacks with interleukin-1 blockade using anakinra or canakinumab as the mainstay of disease-specific therapy
Use TNF inhibition or interleukin-6 blockade with tocilizumab in selected cases refractory to interleukin-1 blockade
Treat acute flares symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or short corticosteroid courses
Undertake surveillance for secondary AA amyloidosis through proteinuria monitoring, maintaining tight control of inflammation
Support the severe mevalonic aciduria end of the spectrum with neurodevelopmental, ophthalmological, and physiotherapy care, considering haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in refractory disease
Manage triggers by treating intercurrent infection and anticipating vaccination-related flares
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance of MVK variants and manage through rheumatology and immunology
